extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychology/psychoanalysis, literary theory, and humour studies
extracted.subtask_short: theory of jokes and the comic
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic/psychoanalytic account of what makes something a joke versus merely comic, listing techniques (degradation, unmasking, parody, mimicry, faulty reasoning, comparison) and psychological mechanisms (unconscious vs preconscious localization; difference in expenditure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degradation
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The occasion of the Ludicrous is the Degradation of some person or interest, possessing dignity, in circumstances that excite no other strong emotion.’ Degradation makes something exalted appear commonplace or inferior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs by reducing dignity or elevating the commonplace; produces laughter by sparing the listener the 'increased expenditure of the solemn restraint' and discharging the difference. Techniques that effect degradation include caricature, parody, travesty, representation by the opposite, and certain comparisons (e.g., comparing the sublime with the commonplace). Example: anecdote where an aristocratic lady’s cry is exposed as ordinary ('Ah! mon Dieu!' vs 'Aa-ee, aa-ee!'). Note linguistic usage: ordinary speech may call many such devices 'jokes' even when they function as comic degradation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference in expenditure (ideational mimetics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic pleasure arises from a comparison between two expenditures (efforts) of understanding or ideational mimetics; laughter discharges the difference in expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by bodily innervation when contemplating the sublime (solemn restraint) versus a degraded conception where that restraint is unnecessary; when a previously 'habitual' ideational method is contrasted with a new one, the comparison creates a discharge (laughter). This principle underlies mimicry, comparison, and other comic effects. Use when analyzing whether an effect is comic: ask what expenditures are being compared and whether relief/discharge results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature (isolation and exaggeration of a single trait)
rubrics_metrics.description: Caricature brings about degradation by emphasizing in the general impression given by the exalted object a single trait which is comic in itself but was bound to be overlooked so long as it was only perceivable in the general picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By isolating or exaggerating a trait, caricature can create a comic effect that extends in memory over the whole object; it may even falsify reality (invent a comic trait) without diminishing effect. Condition: the actual presence of the exalted object must not keep us in a reverential attitude. Example: turning a prominent person into a comic figure by exaggerating one overlooked trait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody and Travesty (destroying unity of character and speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parody and travesty degrade by destroying the unity between people's characters and their speeches/actions, replacing exalted figures or utterances with inferior ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguished from caricature in method, but similar in their production of comic pleasure. Often used to unmask those who have seized dignity by deception. Works when the replacement exposes incongruity between expected dignity and actual expression or behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unmasking (revealing common frailties and psychical automatism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unmasking degrades dignity by directing attention to frailties shared with all humanity, especially dependence of mental functions on bodily needs, or revealing monotonous psychical automatism behind apparent freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May serve as façade for a deeper joke or itself be a comic story rather than a joke. Examples: marriage-broker anecdotes that expose automatisms; stories that reveal how admired people are 'only human'. Unmasking sometimes combines with other joke-techniques (e.g., representation by the opposite). Linguistic usage often labels such exposures as 'jokes' even when they function as comic unmasking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation by the opposite
rubrics_metrics.description: A technique where someone attempts to establish one thing but ends up proving the opposite (representation by the opposite), used as a joke-device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a marriage-broker trying to prove a family is rich but proving they are poor. When combined with unmasking, this becomes a clear joke rather than only a comic story. Useful diagnostic: look for statements that, in trying to assert a positive, simultaneously assert its negation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of unconscious modes / Faulty reasoning (nonsensical jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes often give free play to modes of thought usual in the unconscious but judged 'faulty reasoning' in conscious thought; they may appear as nonsense before conscious criticism but rely on unconscious revision to restore meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: a compromise between criticism and the urge for wordplay/nonsense. Jokes may disguise faulty reasoning under a show of logic to avoid objection; if the faulty reasoning is presented undisguised it appears nonsensical and provokes criticism, yet can still produce comic pleasure because of the contrast with its conscious correction. Examples: anecdotes showing mutually cancelling assertions (borrowed kettle with a hole). Distinguish whether the faulty reasoning is concealed (successful joke) or bare (comic or nonsensical effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Janus double-face of the joke
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine joke presents a double face to its hearer: one view (surface wording) that may appear nonsensical or ordinary, and another view which, through unconscious associations or allusion, yields an additional sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'two-view' requirement distinguishes jokes from mere comic phrasing: nonsense jokes satisfy the double-face by having a surface nonsense and a latent sense; 'rudimentary' joke-like productions (e.g., some of Wippchen's amalgamations) often have only one developed face and thus fail to be true jokes. Use the double-face test to decide whether an item is a joke or merely comic nonsense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimicry / mécanisation de la vie (comic of faithfulness and expectation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mimicry provokes laughter particularly by the faithfulness of imitation; Bergson's idea ('mécanisation de la vie') explains that when living things appear mechanized or repeated exactly, we suspect mechanism and laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud reframes this in terms of expenditure: when living multiplicity and plasticity lead us to expect difference, exact conformity causes disappointment of expectation and a relief/discharge (laughter). Mimicry is thus often comic of expectation rather than comic of situation. Consider both faithfulness and the listener's expectation when evaluating mimetic comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison / Analogy (aptness and degradation via economy in abstraction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons and analogies can be comic when they draw attention to a conformity that causes degradation or when an abstract/sublime thing is compared with something commonplace, producing an economy of abstraction and a relief of intellectual work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key attribute is aptness — whether the analogy draws an actually present conformity. The comic arises from the rise in difference between expenditures on abstraction for the two compared objects. Some comparisons are purely jokes (avoid degradation), some are purely comic (degrading), and some combine both. Example: comparing 'memory' to a 'warehouse' is both comic (degradation) and a joke (because of unexpected unification). Evaluate whether comparison reduces a serious/abstract thing to the commonplace and whether ideological/expectational expenditures are relieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between jokes and the comic of speech (comic nonsense vs jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many authorities equate jokes with the comic of speech, but Freud insists on a sharp distinction: the comic of speech is an intentionally evoked comic mood (wit), while a joke is a psychological product rooted in the unconscious and typically has the double-face structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Stettenheim’s 'Wippchen' letters are full of comic speech (wit) and comic nonsense but many of their joke-like items lack the unconscious-latent side and thus are not true jokes. Diagnosis: ask whether the effect is produced by abundant comic phrasing/wit (comic of speech) or by the joke-work that mobilizes unconscious processes and double meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadequacy / failure to meet essential conditions as a source of comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute inadequacy — failure to comply with essential conditions of a genre (riddle, poem, argument) — can produce irresistibly comic effects by virtue of being absurdly inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a stupid riddle whose proposed answer is ludicrous (herring for a hand-towel) or badly executed poems (Friederike Kempner) that are comic because of clumsy expression and sincerity. The comic may arise either from exposing unconscious modes or from contrast with what a proper performance ought to effect. Consider the role of sincerity and the gap between intention and execution: great distance from expected standard tends toward comic rather than merely annoying, especially if sincerity disarms ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychical localization: joke in the unconscious vs comic in preconscious
rubrics_metrics.description: Freud locates jokes in the realm of the unconscious, whereas comic pleasure generally stems from comparisons assignable to the preconscious; this psychical localization distinguishes jokes from general comic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: look for mechanisms tied to unconscious processes (double meanings, slips, repressed associations) to classify something as a joke; if the effect relies on preconscious economical operations (comparison of expenditures, expectation relief) it is more likely the comic. This is a theoretical diagnostic principle rather than a surface stylistic test.
